prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.

A minor aged sixteen or above who drives an electric bicycle shall not carry any passenger. When carrying goods on an electric bicycle, the relevant provisions of laws and regulations shall be observed. Article 22 A safety helmet shall be worn by persons driving or riding on an electric bicycle in accordance with the规定. The specific time and area for implementation shall be determined by the people’s government of the city with districts. Article 23 When driving an electric bicycle on the road, the following provisions shall be observed: (1) travel in the non-motor vehicle lane; where there is no non-motor vehicle lane, travel along the right side of the roadway; (2) when traveling in a non-motor vehicle lane, the speed shall not exceed fifteen kilometers per hour; (3) obey traffic signals, traffic signs, and traffic markings, and comply with the directions of traffic police; (4) when facing a red light, wait in order within the non-motor vehicle lane stop line or the waiting/turning area; (5) slow down and keep a lookout before turning, and yield to vehicles going straight and to pedestrians when turning; (6) slow down when passing a pedestrian crossing, and stop and yield when pedestrians are crossing; (7) when passing roads without traffic signals, yield to pedestrians crossing the road; (8) when traveling at night or in rain, snow, fog, haze, or other low-visibility conditions, turn on the lights and slow down; (9) other provisions of laws and regulations concerning travel in non-motor vehicle lanes. When driving an electric bicycle on the road, one shall not drive in the wrong direction, tow animals, hold objects in hand, browse electronic devices, or engage in other conduct affecting safe driving, and shall not enter areas where non-motor vehicles are prohibited. Drunk driving of electric bicycles is prohibited. Article 24 Where an electric bicycle cannot travel within its own lane because the non-motor vehicle lane is occupied, and it uses an adjacent motor vehicle lane to pass through the obstructed section, motor vehicles shall slow down and yield. When electric bicycles and motor vehicles meet at night on narrow roads or narrow bridges, motor vehicles shall use low-beam headlights. At intersections without traffic signal control or traffic police direction, turning motor vehicles shall yield to electric bicycles going straight. Article 25 Electric bicycles parked in public places shall be parked in an orderly manner within non-motor vehicle parking areas. Where no non-motor vehicle parking area is provided, electric bicycles shall not occupy blind lanes or sidewalks, shall not impede the passage of other vehicles or pedestrians, and shall not affect the urban appearance and environment. Electronic devices shall not be used by hand, and no other conduct that impedes safe driving of a non-motor vehicle shall be engaged in; passengers shall sit facing forward and shall not hold umbrellas; 2. When passing through an intersection controlled by traffic signals, passage shall be in sequence; where vehicles or pedestrians that were given priority to proceed have not yet cleared the intersection, they shall be allowed to pass first; 3. When passing bus stops, schools, hospitals, and similar sections, speed shall be reduced and pedestrians shall be avoided with caution; 4. When passing a pedestrian crossing, speed shall be reduced; where pedestrians are crossing the pedestrian crossing, the vehicle shall stop and yield; 5. Vehicle Traffic System 2 Vehicle Traffic System 2.1 Vehicle Traffic Space Scale The longitudinal and transverse road space occupied by vehicular traffic is referred to as vehicle traffic space. Generally speaking, vehicle traffic space includes carriageways, bus-only lanes, medians, and roadside parking lanes. Figure 2.1-1 Components of Vehicle Traffic Space 2.1.1 Motor Vehicle Lane The width of a motor vehicle lane shall include the carriageway width and the curb lane widths on both sides. Where a single carriageway road or a three-carriageway road uses a central separator or double yellow lines to separate opposing traffic, the pavement width of the motor vehicle lane shall also include the width of the separator or double yellow lines. 1. Running Lane The width of a running lane is related to the road design speed. The recommended width for urban road running lanes is 3.25 m–3.5 m. 2. Two-Way Single Lane Where a lower-grade branch road is designed as a single lane permitting two-way travel, the width shall be 4.5 m. The subgrade width for sections with passing bays shall not be less than 6.5 m. 3. Bus-Only Lane The recommended width of a bus-only lane is 3.5 m. At bus stops, the lane width shall be 3 m. 27 Figure 2.1-2 Typical Lane Width Settings 2.1.2 Tidal Lane In response to the “tidal phenomenon” of traffic, lanes may be provided on road sections whose direction of travel can be changed according to traffic flow demand. In addition, the control center may monitor intersection conditions through instruments and, when appropriate, use remote control means to control signboards; where intersection signal controllers are connected in a computer network, they may also be identified through an automatic recognition system and automatically regulated. Figure 2.1-3 Tidal Lane and Movable Barrier 2.1.3 Shared Lane 1. The design concept of shared roads emphasizes the integration of sidewalk and motor vehicle lane space. The use of shared-road space is pedestrian-oriented. In terms of functional space, it meets the different needs of different groups, including walking, cycling, and motor vehicles. In terms of planning concept, shared roads emphasize people-centered design, serving pedestrians and providing convenience for urban residents, making them more willing to gather in shared-road spaces.
